content.doc_md:
The.gitignorefile tells Git which files and folders to ignore (not track).

This is useful for keeping log files, temporary files, build artifacts, or personal files out of your repository.

The.gitignorefile itselfistracked by Git, so everyone using the repository ignores the same files.

To ignore a folder and everything inside it, use a trailing slash:

This ignores any folder namedtempanywhere in your project.

Wildcards let you match many files or folders at once:

Use!tonotignore something that would otherwise be ignored. This is called an exception:

This ignores all.logfiles exceptimportant.log.

Lines starting with#are comments and are ignored by Git. Blank lines are also ignored. Use comments to explain your rules:

If you want to ignore files only for yourself (not for everyone who uses the repository), add them to.git/info/exclude. This works just like.gitignorebut is not shared.

You can set up a global.gitignorefile for all your projects. This is great for ignoring OS or editor files everywhere (like.DS_StoreorThumbs.db):

Then add your patterns to~/.gitignore_global.

If you add a file to.gitignorebut Git is still tracking it, you need to tell Git to stop:

This removes the file from the repository but keeps it on your computer. Next time you commit, Git will ignore it.

Here are some common patterns and how they match:

### Code Snippets

```
temp/

---

*.tmp      # all .tmp files
my?ile.txt # matches my1ile.txt, myAile.txt, etc.
log[0-9].txt # log1.txt, log2.txt, ... log9.txt

---

*.log
!important.log

---

# Ignore log files
*.log

# Ignore temp folders
temp/
```
